curriculumDefinition.learningOutcome: Select the smallest reliable motion for nearby punctuation, repeated text, matching delimiters, sentences, and paragraphs
curriculumDefinition.representativeExercises: Delete until a quote; repeat a comma find; change the next search match; jump between brackets; move by paragraphs in prose or comments
curriculumDefinition.priorityAndPortability: Core. Search and pair matching remain text-based rather than IDE-semantic

lessons.title: Aim at a nearby character
lessons.objective: Choose between landing on a character and stopping just before it in either direction.

activities.title: Find lands; till stops short
activities.body: `f` and `F` land on a chosen character. `t` and `T` stop one character before it, leaving a boundary untouched for a following operator.
activities.grammar: f{char} / F{char} → land · t{char} / T{char} → stop short
activities.contrast: `w` follows word rules; find and till aim at literal characters on the current line.

activities.title: Tour one call by punctuation
activities.instruction: Visit delimiters in both directions, sometimes landing and sometimes stopping short.

commandGroups.explanation: Stop just after the earlier c.

hints: Read the target character after each motion.

feedback.success: Four precise motions, one short line.
feedback.why: Literal-character motions reached punctuation without counting columns.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript call provides natural parentheses and repeated commas.

activities.title: Land on the call boundary
activities.instruction: Move to the closing parenthesis of the call.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the closing parenthesis on this line.

feedback.success: You landed on the boundary.
feedback.why: `f` includes the character it finds.

provenance.languageRationale: A Go-style call gives the closing delimiter a clear local purpose.

activities.title: Keep the safe mode
activities.instruction: Remove the “-debug” suffix from the quoted mode.

commandGroups.explanation: Delete until the quote while preserving it.

feedback.success: The suffix is gone and the quote remains.
feedback.why: `t"` supplied exactly the characterwise range that `d` needed.

provenance.languageRationale: A TypeScript string makes preserving the closing quote meaningful.

activities.title: Replace only the status value
activities.instruction: Replace the status value “pending” with “ready”.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the physical line end.

hints: Move onto the value, then use `c$`.

feedback.success: Only the YAML value changed.
feedback.why: Backward till found the structural boundary without disturbing it.

provenance.languageRationale: A YAML key/value pair gives the colon a stable boundary.

lessons.title: Echo a character find
lessons.objective: Repeat or reverse the most recent character search without retyping its target.

activities.title: Semicolon keeps direction; comma reverses it
activities.body: After `f`, `F`, `t`, or `T`, semicolon repeats the same character search in the same direction. Comma repeats it in the opposite direction.
activities.contrast: The repeat remembers both the target character and the direction of the original find.

activities.title: Walk a comma list
activities.instruction: Find the first comma, continue twice, then reverse once.
hints: Only the first find names the comma.
Use `;` to continue and `,` to reverse.

feedback.success: The same comma target carried across the list.
feedback.why: Find-repeat separates choosing the target from visiting its occurrences.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript argument list naturally repeats commas.

activities.title: Reach the second separator
activities.instruction: Move to the comma after “two”.

feedback.success: One target, two landings.
feedback.why: Semicolon reused the comma and its forward direction.

provenance.languageRationale: A Python list gives repeated separators without extra syntax.

activities.title: Repair both separators
activities.instruction: Replace both semicolons with commas.

feedback.success: Both separators now agree.
feedback.why: The character search and the text change kept separate repeat histories.

provenance.languageRationale: A compact JavaScript fragment makes inconsistent separators obvious.

activities.title: Backtrack through arguments
activities.instruction: Visit the closing parenthesis, backtrack to the comma after “alpha”, then finish on the comma after “beta”.

feedback.success: You reversed the repeated find deliberately.
feedback.why: The meaning of `;` and `,` comes from the original find direction.

provenance.languageRationale: A Rust-style call makes both comma targets unambiguous.

lessons.title: Search beyond the current line
lessons.objective: Start forward or backward searches and repeat them in the intended direction.

activities.title: A search establishes a direction
activities.body: `/` searches forward and `?` searches backward. Afterward, `n` repeats that search direction and `N` goes the opposite way.
activities.grammar: /pattern Enter or ?pattern Enter → n continues → N reverses
activities.contrast: Character finds stay on one line; pattern searches cross line boundaries and wrap the buffer.

activities.title: Inspect repeated deployment states
activities.instruction: Search forward for `draft`, move among matches, then search backward for `ready`.

commandGroups.explanation: Start a backward search for ready.

hints: `n` follows the established direction; `N` opposes it.

feedback.success: You controlled both the pattern and its direction.
feedback.why: Search history let short repeat keys navigate distant matches.

provenance.languageRationale: YAML-like state rows provide repeated, realistic search tokens.

activities.title: Find the first timeout
activities.instruction: Find the first “timeout” setting.

feedback.success: The first matching setting is selected.
feedback.why: A pattern search crossed the line boundary directly.

provenance.languageRationale: TOML-style settings make a repeated timeout key natural.

activities.title: Return to the latest error
activities.instruction: Find the most recent “ERROR” row above the cursor.

commandGroups.explanation: Search backward for the nearest error.

hints: The target is above the cursor.

feedback.success: You returned to the latest error.
feedback.why: Backward search selected the nearest earlier match.

provenance.languageRationale: Logs naturally reward searching upward for the latest failure.

activities.title: Advance, then reconsider
activities.instruction: Move forward to the final “cache” row, then back to the preceding match.

feedback.success: You navigated search history in both directions.
feedback.why: `n` and `N` reused one pattern without retyping it.

provenance.languageRationale: Python-like cache rows make repeated identifiers easy to inspect.

lessons.title: Search the word under the cursor
lessons.objective: Choose whole-word or substring matching without typing the pattern.

activities.title: The cursor can supply the pattern
activities.body: `*` and `#` search forward or backward for the whole word under the cursor. `g*` and `g#` use the same text but also allow it inside a larger word.
activities.contrast: Whole-word search avoids matching `cat` inside `scatter`; the g-prefixed forms deliberately allow it.

activities.title: Compare whole words with substrings
activities.instruction: Search `cat` as a whole word in both directions, then include the occurrence inside `scatter`.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the next whole word cat.
Return to the previous whole word cat.
Return to the final whole word.

hints: Plain star commands respect word boundaries.

feedback.success: Whole-word and substring searches are now distinct.
feedback.why: The command variant expressed whether surrounding letters mattered.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral text isolates the boundary difference between cat and scatter.

activities.title: Find the next token declaration
activities.instruction: Find the next complete “token” word.

commandGroups.explanation: Search forward for the current whole word.

hints: The cursor is already on the pattern.

feedback.success: The next token declaration is selected.
feedback.why: Star avoided opening and typing into the search prompt.

provenance.languageRationale: A repeated TypeScript identifier is a natural whole-word target.

activities.title: Return to the earlier ready state
activities.instruction: Return to the previous complete “ready” word.

commandGroups.explanation: Search backward for the current whole word.

feedback.success: You reached the earlier ready row.
feedback.why: Hash reused the cursor word while searching backward.

provenance.languageRationale: Short YAML-like states keep the whole-word target clear.

activities.title: Find cat inside the larger word
activities.instruction: Move back to the “cat” inside “scatter”.
hints: Plain `#` would prefer the earlier standalone word.

feedback.success: You found the embedded substring.
feedback.why: `g#` deliberately ignored the larger word boundary.

provenance.languageRationale: The cat/scatter contrast makes substring matching immediately visible.

lessons.title: Treat a match as a range
lessons.objective: Select or change the next or previous search match with gn and gN.

activities.title: A search match can be the motion
activities.body: `gn` selects the next match and `gN` selects the previous match. With an operator, forms such as `cgn` and `cgN` act on that exact match.
activities.grammar: search → gn / gN · operator + gn / gN
activities.contrast: Unlike `n` and `N`, the directions of `gn` and `gN` do not depend on whether the last search began with `/` or `?`.

activities.title: Select and change matches in both directions
activities.instruction: Search backward, select the previous match with `gN`, change it, then select the next match with `gn` and change that too.

commandGroups.explanation: Establish the draft pattern with a backward search.
Select the previous match, independent of the earlier search direction.

hints: Move off a match before choosing its direction.
`gN` is always backward; `gn` is always forward.
A Visual match can be changed with `c`.

feedback.success: Two exact matches changed in opposite directions.
feedback.why: Search supplied the pattern while gn and gN supplied deterministic ranges.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral repeated states expose match ranges without language syntax.

activities.title: Select matches in both directions
activities.instruction: Visit the final “draft”, return to the previous “keep”, then finish at the period after the last match.

commandGroups.explanation: Search backward to the final draft.

hints: Move off the current match before choosing a direction.
`gN` is backward and `gn` is forward, regardless of the earlier `?`.
Escape cancels each Visual selection without changing text.

feedback.success: Both match directions selected exactly one result.
feedback.why: The ordered match ranges stayed independent of the original search direction.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral repeated text exposes both Visual match ranges without an unrelated edit.

activities.title: Promote the next draft
activities.instruction: Change the next “draft” after the cursor to “live”.

feedback.success: Only the intended match changed.
feedback.why: `gn` gave `c` the complete match range.

provenance.languageRationale: A Python-like state sequence makes one exact replacement easy to verify.

activities.title: Change the match behind you
activities.instruction: Change the previous “draft” before the cursor to “live”.

feedback.success: The previous match became live.
feedback.why: `cgN` selected the nearest earlier match even though the cursor was between matches.

provenance.languageRationale: A YAML-like repeated state keeps the backward target unambiguous.

activities.title: Keep gn pointing forward
activities.instruction: After searching backward, change the final “draft” to “live”.

commandGroups.explanation: Search backward to the final draft.
Change the next match; gn remains forward.

hints: From `keep`, the next draft is to the right.

feedback.success: gn stayed forward after a backward search.
feedback.why: Match-motion direction is fixed by `n` versus `N` in the command itself.

provenance.languageRationale: A log-like sequence isolates the direction rule that differs from ordinary n/N.

lessons.title: Cross a matching pair
lessons.objective: Use percent to reach or operate through an unambiguous paired delimiter.

activities.title: Percent follows the matching delimiter
activities.body: On a parenthesis, bracket, or brace, `%` jumps to its partner. Before a delimiter, it finds the next delimiter on the line and follows that pair.
activities.contrast: Percent is text-based pair matching, not an IDE-aware structural query.

activities.title: Cross nested call boundaries
activities.instruction: Find the outer parenthesis and cross it, then find the inner bracket backward and cross that pair.

commandGroups.explanation: Land on the outer opening parenthesis.
Find the inner opening bracket backward.

hints: Percent chooses its matching partner, even with nesting.

feedback.success: Both nested pairs stayed correctly matched.
feedback.why: Percent followed pair structure instead of searching for a literal closing symbol.

provenance.languageRationale: A TypeScript call with indexed data provides clear nested parentheses and brackets.

activities.title: Reach the block close
activities.instruction: Move from the opening brace to its matching closing brace.

commandGroups.explanation: Follow the opening brace to its partner.

feedback.success: You reached the matching block boundary.
feedback.why: Percent crossed lines while preserving delimiter nesting.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript block makes the brace relationship explicit.

activities.title: Remove the temporary argument list
activities.instruction: Remove the complete “(temp)” argument list.
hints: Percent can be an operator motion.

feedback.success: The complete argument list is gone.
feedback.why: The inclusive pair motion gave delete both delimiters and their contents.

provenance.languageRationale: A minimal Go-style call makes the inclusive d% range obvious.

activities.title: Jump through the inline block
activities.instruction: Move through the inline block to its closing brace.

commandGroups.explanation: Find the next delimiter, then jump to its match.

hints: You do not have to stand on the brace.
Percent scans to the next delimiter on this line.

feedback.success: You crossed the inline block in one motion.
feedback.why: Percent first located the opening brace and then resolved its pair.

provenance.languageRationale: A compact C-style block demonstrates percent's next-delimiter behavior.

lessons.title: Move through prose structure
lessons.objective: Navigate sentence starts and blank-line paragraph boundaries in prose and comments.

activities.title: Punctuation and blank lines form larger landmarks
activities.body: `(` and `)` move between sentence starts. `{` and `}` move between paragraph boundaries, usually marked by empty lines.
activities.contrast: These motions use Vim's text rules; they do not infer semantic paragraphs from code structure.

activities.title: Tour sentences and paragraphs
activities.instruction: Move to the next sentence and back, then cross paragraph boundaries in both directions.

lines: Third paragraph starts here. Another ends?
Third paragraph starts here. Another ends?

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the next sentence start.
Return to the previous sentence start.

lines: Third paragraph starts here. Another ends?

hints: Curly braces follow blank-line paragraph structure.

feedback.success: You navigated two levels of prose structure.
feedback.why: Sentence and paragraph motions used landmarks larger than words or lines.

provenance.languageRationale: Neutral prose exposes Vim's sentence punctuation and blank-line paragraph rules.

activities.title: Reach the next sentence
activities.instruction: Move to the start of the next sentence, “Beta begins.”

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the next sentence start.

feedback.success: You reached the next sentence start.
feedback.why: The motion recognized punctuation followed by whitespace as a boundary.

provenance.languageRationale: A Markdown sentence pair keeps the punctuation boundary compact.

activities.title: Return to the earlier sentence
activities.instruction: Move back to the start of “Beta!”.

commandGroups.explanation: Move to the previous sentence start.

feedback.success: You returned to the previous sentence.
feedback.why: Backward sentence motion landed at the start after the earlier punctuation.

provenance.languageRationale: Short neutral prose makes the previous sentence start unmistakable.

activities.title: Cross two paragraph boundaries
activities.instruction: Move forward across two paragraph boundaries to the blank line before “last line”.

commandGroups.explanation: Move forward across two paragraph boundaries.

feedback.success: You crossed the paragraph and reached the buffer end.
feedback.why: The count repeated the structural motion rather than counting lines.

provenance.languageRationale: Markdown-like paragraphs provide a natural empty-line separator.

lessons.title: Choose the smallest reliable target
lessons.objective: Combine nearby character motions, searches, match ranges, and delimiter pairs deliberately.

activities.title: Let distance and structure choose the motion
activities.body: Use find or till for a visible character on the current line, search for repeated text across the buffer, and percent for a known delimiter pair. Match motions are best when the search result itself is the range.
activities.grammar: nearby character → f/t · repeated text → search · paired delimiter → %
activities.contrast: The shortest command is not dependable if it targets the wrong kind of structure.

activities.title: Search for a call and inspect its boundary
activities.instruction: Search for `build`, find its opening parenthesis, then jump to the matching close.

commandGroups.explanation: Follow the pair to the close.

hints: Use search for the repeated name.

feedback.success: Three target shapes, three fitting motions.
feedback.why: Each motion handled the structure it describes most reliably.

provenance.languageRationale: Repeated TypeScript calls support a natural search-find-pair workflow.

activities.title: Cut the draft suffix cleanly
activities.instruction: Remove the “-post” suffix from the quoted slug.

feedback.success: The draft suffix remains and the extra suffix is gone.
feedback.why: Find plus operator-till made a precise, delimiter-safe edit.

provenance.languageRationale: The established JavaScript cut-vine scenario directly represents the curriculum example.

activities.title: Inspect the build arguments
activities.instruction: Find the “build” call, visit its opening parenthesis, then finish on the matching close.

commandGroups.explanation: Search across lines for the call.

hints: Search gets to the correct line.

feedback.success: You moved from global retrieval to local structure.
feedback.why: The composed navigation avoided repeated horizontal and vertical taps.

provenance.languageRationale: A Python-like call list makes long-range search and local delimiter matching complementary.

activities.title: Replace the searched value
activities.instruction: Find “legacy” and replace it with “ready”, preserving the quotes.

commandGroups.explanation: Enter the replacement and return to Normal.

hints: The cursor lands inside the quotes.

feedback.success: The searched value changed without disturbing its quote.
feedback.why: Search retrieved the target and till preserved its delimiter.

provenance.languageRationale: A JavaScript configuration value combines realistic retrieval with a precise quote boundary.

activities.title: Choose the structural motion
activities.prompt: The cursor is on an opening parenthesis in a nested call. Which command most reliably reaches its matching close?
activities.explanation: `%` follows the matching pair, while `f)` can stop at an inner closing parenthesis.

activities.title: Target the text you can describe
activities.body: Nearby characters, repeated patterns, matching pairs, and prose boundaries each have a motion designed for their shape.
takeaways: `f/F/t/T` target literal characters on the current line; `;` and `,` reuse that target.
`/`, `?`, `n`, `N`, and cursor-word searches retrieve text across the buffer.
`gn/gN` turn matches into ranges, `%` follows pairs, and sentence or paragraph motions follow text landmarks.

reference.purpose: Find a literal character on the current line, landing on it or stopping short.
notes: Lowercase searches forward; uppercase searches backward.
Till motions preserve the target character.

reference.purpose: Repeat the last character find in the same or opposite direction.
Search for an explicit pattern and revisit its matches.
notes: n follows the original search direction.

reference.purpose: Search for the word under the cursor without typing it.
notes: g* and g# also match inside larger words.

reference.purpose: Select or operate on the next or previous search match.
notes: gn is always forward and gN always backward.
They can complete operators such as cgn and cgN.

reference.purpose: Jump to the matching parenthesis, bracket, or brace.
notes: On earlier text, percent first finds the next delimiter on the line.
The behavior is text-based rather than IDE-semantic.

reference.purpose: Move to previous or next sentence starts.
notes: Sentence boundaries follow Vim punctuation and whitespace rules.

reference.purpose: Move backward or forward across paragraph boundaries.
notes: Empty lines form the dependable paragraph boundaries used in this unit.
